clue.text: Place sounds suitable for those watching their weight

indicators.note: sounds tells the solver to say a phrase out loud and hear another spelling in it

parts.words: suitable for those watching their weight
parts.note: low-cal food is low in calories, fit for dieters

explanation.surface: A venue or eatery that suits slimmers, such as a diet restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: LOW-CAL, short for low-calorie, said aloud gives LOCALE.
explanation.definitionFit: A locale is a site or setting where something happens, a close synonym of place.

clue.text: Insane to reshuffle so many in this government

indicators.note: a cabinet reshuffle moves people around, so the preceding letters are moved into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dig at a prime minister whose cabinet reshuffle is mad, given how many ministers went to the same school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Insane to reshuffle' reads as a verdict, but 'to' belongs to the letters being shuffled. Eton is the English public school that produced many Conservative ministers.
explanation.definitionFit: Former pupils of Eton College have been numerous in recent British cabinets, so the definition describes a familiar political complaint.

clue.text: Gloomy ballad going only halfway round the world

indicators.note: going only halfway means each word stops at its midpoint, keeping its front portion

parts.note: the first half of the word
the first half of the word

explanation.surface: A sad song that only makes it partway on a world tour.
explanation.definitionFit: Something global extends across the whole planet, which is what round the world means as an adjective.

clue.text: It covered what cockneys believe …

parts.note: surface: something concealed a thing; setter's reading: the leaf Adam wore over his private parts
surface: a cockney's faith; setter's reading: cockney rhyming slang works by rhyme, and the answer rhymes with belief

explanation.surface: Something hid what Londoners hold to be true, leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: A whimsical play: the leaf from Genesis covered nakedness, and as a phrase it rhymes with 'belief', as cockney rhyming slang might use it. The ellipsis runs on to 5 down.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Adam and Eve sewed leaves of this tree to cover their nakedness, so the plant part is what covered them.

clue.text: … a brave statement, certainly

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a declaration of being unafraid
second meaning: a colloquial British exclamation of emphatic refusal, as in certainly not

explanation.surface: Continuing 4 down: a courageous declaration, said with conviction.
explanation.walkthrough: As a British exclamation the phrase means 'certainly not!', a strong emphatic reply, which the clue shortens to 'certainly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying you have no fright is a show of bravery, and the same two words serve as an emphatic informal retort.

clue.text: Dizzy blonde holding one a place in Oxford

indicators.note: holding means wrapping around, so the following pieces sit inside the rest
someone dizzy is giddy and spinning, so the word beside it is set whirling into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scatter-brained blonde carrying a single item somewhere in Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bodleian is the main research library of Oxford University.
explanation.definitionFit: The library is a famous building and institution of the university city, so it is a location there.

clue.text: Serious offence for those who die at home

parts.note: mortals are beings subject to death
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: A grave crime committed by people who pass away in their own houses.
explanation.definitionFit: In Catholic teaching a mortal sin is a grave wrongdoing that cuts the soul off from grace.

clue.text: Set to in fight may result in a thick lip

definitions.text: may result in a thick lip
definitions.note: describes the answer by an effect of its use

indicators.note: to set something in a place is to put it inside, here inside the word for a fight

parts.note: to box is to fight with fists
taken as written

explanation.surface: A set-to, a scuffle, during a fight could leave you with a swollen mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set to' reads as one noun meaning a brawl, but 'Set' is the instruction and 'to' the letters to be placed.
explanation.definitionFit: Botulinum toxin injections are used cosmetically to plump lips, so the treatment can leave a swollen-looking mouth.

clue.text: They are what they eat — and vice versa?

definitions.text: They are what they eat — and vice versa?

parts.note: surface: the saying you are what you eat, about diet
setter's reading: they also eat what they are, namely their own species

explanation.surface: A twist on the health slogan that diet shapes who you are.
explanation.walkthrough: Reversing the slogan gives people who eat people.
explanation.definitionFit: Cannibals eat members of their own species, so they literally consume what they themselves are.

clue.text: Sweet Doctor Jekyll removing baker's heart

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are rearranged
removing means taking something away from the name before it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter

parts.note: the central letter of the five-letter word

explanation.surface: The kindly Dr Jekyll cutting out a baker's heart, a horror story in a bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor Jekyll' looks like Stevenson's character, but 'Doctor' is the anagram signal. Remove K from JEKYLL and rearrange JEYLL.
explanation.definitionFit: Jelly is a sweet dessert of set fruit-flavoured gelatin, served as a pudding in Britain.

clue.text: Standard of fitness once seen in circuses

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the creature in the simile 'fit as a ___'
second meaning: performers in old-time miniature insect circuses

explanation.surface: A benchmark of physical condition that used to be shown off by circus performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit as a flea' is a British simile for very healthy; flea circuses were Victorian fairground novelties.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiny jumping insect is the comparison in a common simile for good health and also starred in historic flea circuses.

clue.text: Set out to find wherein the devil may be hiding

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a verb, to list or describe fully

definitions.text: wherein the devil may be hiding
definitions.meaning: second meaning: from the proverb that the devil is in the fine points

explanation.surface: An exorcist starting out to locate where Satan is lurking.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the devil is in the detail' warns that problems hide in small points.
explanation.definitionFit: To detail is to set out item by item, and a detail is a small particular, where the proverb places the devil.

clue.text: Reacting badly to a display of ill grace

indicators.note: a display arranges things for show, so the letters that follow are laid out afresh

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who responds sulkily to bad manners.
explanation.definitionFit: Being allergic means the body responds with an adverse immune reaction to a substance.

clue.text: He's inside returning pint — it avoids any further issue

indicators.note: inside means placed within, so one piece goes into another
returning means going back, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A man in a pub sends back his beer to avoid any more complaints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' here means offspring. HES goes inside TNIP, the reversed pint.
explanation.definitionFit: The snip is British slang for a vasectomy, an operation preventing the man fathering more children, his issue.

clue.text: Raise the hinge in error

indicators.note: something in error is wrongly set up, so these letters must be put into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A carpenter lifting a door by the wrong fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: To heighten is to make higher or increase, matching raise as a verb.

clue.text: Not certain when second judge drops off

indicators.note: drops off means falls away, so one letter leaves the word for the moment

parts.note: a jiffy is a moment, an instant
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: Uncertainty arises when a second judge nods off in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' is a noun meaning a brief instant, not a number. Remove J from JIFFY to leave IFFY.
explanation.definitionFit: Iffy is an informal adjective for doubtful or uncertain, as in an iffy forecast.

clue.text: Is it too good for criminally bad art?

definitions.text: Is it too good for criminally bad
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the punishment people say is too good for the worst offenders
second meaning: the display of pictures on a gallery wall

explanation.surface: An outraged critic asks whether some dreadful paintings deserve execution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminally bad art' reads as one phrase about awful pictures; split it, and the first part is the saying 'hanging's too good for him'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both execution by the rope and the displaying of pictures in an exhibition.

clue.text: Come on to appreciate novel

parts.note: to get a joke is to appreciate it
something novel is new or fresh

explanation.surface: An instruction to start enjoying a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, but here it is the adjective meaning new.
explanation.definitionFit: To get fresh is informal for making cheeky sexual advances, the same as to come on to someone.

clue.text: Waste a shot taking on poor header, initially

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: taking means taking in, so the word for an attempt holds the other letters

parts.note: to have a shot is to have a try

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the words just before it

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A footballer wastes a chance by attempting a weak header.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Header' looks like football, but it is just one of three words supplying an opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To atrophy is to waste away, as a muscle shrinks from disuse.

clue.text: Pervert is shifty and having a tantrum

indicators.note: to pervert is to twist or distort, so the following letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shady character who looks evasive and is throwing a fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pervert' reads as a noun for a creep but works as a verb meaning distort.
explanation.definitionFit: A hissy fit is an informal name for a childish outburst of temper, the same thing as a tantrum.

clue.text: It's daft to post up identical content

indicators.note: content means what something holds, so the letters sit within the words before it

parts.note: spans the end of post, all of up, and the start of identical

explanation.surface: Posting the same material twice online is foolish.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupid and daft are both everyday adjectives for foolish or lacking sense.

clue.text: Memorable hook needed before melody's end

parts.note: a catch is a hook or fastening

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A songwriting tip: you need a hook before the tune ends to make a song stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hook' looks like the songwriter's sense, a catchy phrase, but here it is a fastening.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchy tune is one that is easily remembered, so catchy means memorable.

clue.text: Smart companion in relaxed clothing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the word that partners smart in the dress code smart-___

explanation.surface: A well-dressed partner seen in comfortable clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart casual' is a dress code between formal and informal, so the answer is smart's usual partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Casual dress is informal everyday wear, and the word is paired with smart in a familiar dress-code phrase.

clue.text: Boss working face-to-face

parts.note: the head is the person in charge
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A manager at work meeting staff in person.
explanation.definitionFit: Head-on describes a direct confrontation front to front, the same as face-to-face.

clue.text: Monster emerging from turbulent lough

indicators.note: turbulent water is churned up, so the letters of the next word are churned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A beast rising from a choppy Irish lake, like a Loch Ness tale.
explanation.walkthrough: A lough is an Irish lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghoul is an evil spirit of folklore that feeds on corpses, a kind of monster.

clue.text: A great run for sexy strip show

parts.note: hot is slang for sexually attractive
to streak is to run naked in public

explanation.surface: A racy striptease act enjoys a long successful season.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot streak is a sustained spell of success, as a winning run in sport or gambling.

clue.text: Regularly order swift response to failure

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A demand that someone always order a quick reaction when things go wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: A resit is a British term for retaking an exam you failed.
explanation.definitionFit: Students who fail an exam are usually offered another sitting, so retaking it is the standard remedy for failing.

clue.text: Insult during happy hour?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an unfair or spiteful remark
second meaning: a drink sold at a reduced price in a bar's discount period

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: a shot of spirits costs less during a bar's happy hour.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheap shot is an unfair, mean-spirited remark aimed at someone, which is a kind of insult.
